characterList.description: A man with short gray hair and a beard, wearing a light blue t-shirt, seated in a beige armchair in front of a desk. Background includes a bookcase filled with books and photos.

content_metadata.description: A video focusing on the significance of using molecular models to understand organic chemistry structures and nomenclature.

qAndA.question: What color is the atom representing nitrogen in the molecular model?
What is the name of the functional group after the modification?

qAndA.answer: Removing two hydrogens attached to the nitrogen
qAndA.question: What is the first step in modifying the amine molecule?

qAndA.answer: Educational and engaging. The speaker's enthusiasm for the subject matter and the use of visual aids contribute to a positive learning experience.
qAndA.question: What is the overall mood of the video?

qAndA.answer: The presence of a double bond between a carbon and an oxygen atom in the amide group, represented by a shorter, bended connector in the model.
qAndA.question: What is the specific detail that visually distinguishes an amide from an amine in the molecular model?

activities.description: Col Harrison starts talking about molecular models.
Col Harrison holds a molecular model.
Col Harrison explains the molecular model.
Col Harrison modifies the molecular model.

scenes.contextualRelevance: This section of the video is relevant for students or individuals interested in understanding organic chemistry through molecular visualization.

narrativeProgression.description: Col Harrison starts talking about the importance of looking at molecular models.
Col Harrison shows a molecular model and explains how to modify it.
Col Harrison identifies the molecular model as pentane amine and points out the amine group.
Col Harrison starts modifying the model to turn it into an amide.
Col Harrison shows the modified model and explains it's now an amide group.
Col Harrison points out the carbon chain and identifies the functional group as a CON group.
Col Harrison explains how methyl or ethyl groups can be attached to the chain or the nitrogen.
Col Harrison concludes the explanation and mentions there is one more group to look at.

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: The things that I think is really important for you to do is to start when you're looking at the model kits,
take a model that you can start with and see what you need to do to turn it into the next one.
So this was one that we looked at in a previous slide. This is Penn-Tan Amine. So this is the Amine group
because the nitrogen and two hydrogens are attached to a carbon that's only attached to hydrogens.
So therefore to turn it into an Amine, I'm going to need to remove both of those
hydrogens and I'm going to need to use one of my little bendies in order to allow me to create
a double bond I need to attach the oxygen. And when I do this, I will end up with an Amine group.
And this is the only difference between an Amine and an Amine. Same molecule that you've
already looked at previously. Let me just orient it so you can see it. So again we have one,
two, three, four, five. So there are five carbons in this chain. You can see this time the functional
group is a CON group. It's a con. CON is our carbon double bonded oxygen and our nitrogen. This
together is what is forming our Amide functional group. Just as we looked at for the Amines,
you can have methyl or ethyl groups attached somewhere along the chain either to the carbons or
to the nitrogen. And again we would name them the same way. We would give a number for which carbon
they were off, starting with number one being our carbon double bonded to an oxygen. And we would
give it an N if the side chain was attached to the nitrogen. And of course you can have an N
comma N if you have two methyl groups attached here and here. It's getting pretty complex, but at
this point in time in our initial study of nomenclature, this is almost the last group that we need to
look at. Just one more and we'll at least have covered most of the key functional groups for
the nomenclature. Thanks for watching.
